doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Subbing in Maynard Ferguson's band in Buffalo
summary: Willie Maiden, a Westlake classmate, called Jimmy to fill in with Maynard Ferguson's band in Buffalo; Speedy Jones and Jackie Byard were in the rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Was that the small big band with Maynard, or was it a whole—

No actually it was a big band. It was a time that he and what’s his name, that was traveling with him then that was on the road together. He and Maynard would take this chemical or whatever it was. And they would stay out of their minds you know. But the thing is — I can’t think of his name right now.
Yeah, well you probably better not.

But all I’m saying, the important thing is that, I mean this was a highly intellectual man. This was no, you know, peddler or anything like that. I mean he was highly respected as a human being. But that was the only time they were traveling on the road together. Willie Maiden was the straw boss. That’s how I got in the band, because Willie Maiden and I finished Westlake College of Music together in Hollywood you see. And he called me up, they were on their way — in fact they were coming to Buffalo to play a gig, and he had found out that I was in Buffalo. And the trombone player had to go home to bury his dad in Texas. So he called me up and said, “Hey man, I’d like for you to come on over to this club we’re playing and make this gig with us, because we don’t want to show up short a man, because our contract could be voided.”
Yeah. Then they don’t want to pay you.

So at that time we had our jazz showcase going on and I was doing a lot of writing and stuff like that. I said, “Well I haven’t been playing too much, really.” We’d been doing a lot of writing and stuff, and he says, “Look Jim” he says, “I know about you. Please do me that favor.” And I talked with Jeannie, and she says, “Hey, go ahead.” And so I made it. And so I went out to that club that night, and walked in and we sat down. And I had met Maynard before, in Hollywood see. And so when we got ready to hit, I said well here it goes, and where it stops nobody knows, but I’m going to give it the best shot, and everybody’s falling out laughing.
He had some great young trumpet players.
Wooo, yeah. He had this lead trumpet player, who was also a fine educator too. And he was just a wonderful —
And Speedy was on the drums.
And Speedy Jones was playing the drums, and Jackie Byard was playing piano.
So the rhythm section was — a really good band you know, a fantastic band. And we had a lot of fun.
I like big bands. That’s sort of my first experience in jazz.

That’s a powerful experience you know. But I think all the youngsters, if they have an opportunity if they play in the marching band or whatever, have an opportunity to play some big band music, you know, it’s on another level. Even a good strong marching band is a heck of a level too. There’s a heck of a high you know. Or a concert band is a heck of a high. But then you get into a jazz band and it’s like whew.
